text: A Meridian batch accepts at most 500 jobs per submission. Submissions above the cap are rejected with BATCH_TOO_LARGE before any job is queued.
In legacy compatibility mode the batch ceiling rises to 2000 jobs, but ordering guarantees are dropped and duplicate delivery is possible.
Workers retry a failed job up to 3 times by default. Backoff is exponential, starting at 2 seconds and capped at 60 seconds between attempts.
When retries are exhausted the job moves to the dead-letter queue. Dead-letter entries are retained for 14 days and then purged.
The default worker execution timeout is 30 seconds per job attempt. A worker that exceeds it is interrupted and the attempt counts as a failure.
A whole batch must finish within 300 seconds. The batch timer is independent of per-attempt worker timeouts and cannot be extended.
Meridian requires mutual TLS for every worker connection. Service tokens rotate every 24 hours and are never accepted without a valid client certificate.
Bearer tokens alone are rejected at the gateway. The 2026.1 release removed the deprecated token-only listener on port 8443.
In Meridian 2026.1, regional failover between eu-west and us-east is manual and triggered by an operator runbook step.
Starting with Meridian 2026.2, regional failover is automatic: the control plane promotes the standby region after 90 seconds of failed health checks.
Workers expose Prometheus metrics on /metrics. Label cardinality is capped at 10000 series per worker to protect the scrape pipeline.
Distributed tracing uses W3C traceparent headers propagated through the job payload. Sampling defaults to 5 percent of batches.
Upgrading from 2026.1 to 2026.2 requires a schema migration on the queue metadata store. Expect roughly two minutes of write downtime during the migration window.
Rollback from 2026.2 to 2026.1 is supported only before the schema migration runs. After migration, rollback requires restoring the metadata store from backup.
Each workspace may submit at most 50 batches per minute. Rate limiting is enforced per API token and returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.
A single job payload may not exceed 256 KiB. Larger payloads must be offloaded to object storage and referenced by URI.
Every StreamProto frame begins with a 9-byte header: a 24-bit length field, an 8-bit type, 8 bits of flags, and a 31-bit stream identifier.
The 24-bit length field sets the default maximum frame payload size to 16383 octets. Endpoints may raise the limit to 16777215 octets with SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE.
The initial flow-control window is 65535 octets for every stream and for the connection. Receivers increase it with WINDOW_UPDATE frames.
A sender must not transmit DATA frames when the window is zero. Sending anyway is a connection error of type FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR.
Streams carry a weight between 1 and 256. Sibling streams share bandwidth in proportion to their weights.
Stream dependencies form a tree rooted at stream 0. A stream becomes blocked while any of its ancestors is blocked.
Connection errors are signalled with GOAWAY, which carries the last processed stream identifier and an error code.
Stream errors are signalled with RST_STREAM and terminate only the affected stream; the connection stays usable for other streams.
StreamProto 2.1 requires TLS 1.3. The ALPN protocol token is 'sp2'; servers must reject handshakes that offer any earlier TLS version.
For backward compatibility during migration, deployments may also offer ALPN token 'sp1' on a separate listener. That token negotiates StreamProto 2.0 framing.
Version 2.1 adds the PRIORITY_UPDATE frame so a client can reprioritize a stream after it has started. Version 2.0 required aborting and reopening the stream instead.
Server push, present in 2.0, was removed in 2.1 because cache-hit rates in production deployments were too low to justify its complexity.
The default limit is 100 concurrent streams per connection. Servers advertise a different value with SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS.
There is no hard cap on header list size in the specification. Implementations commonly enforce 64 KiB and should document their limit.
Archive objects are not readable online. A restore request makes them available after 3 to 5 hours, and the restored copy expires after a configurable period.
Cool storage bills a minimum storage duration of 30 days. Deleting or moving an object earlier still charges for the full 30 days.
Hot storage has no minimum duration and no retrieval fee. It targets objects read several times per week.
CloudTier provides strong read-after-write consistency for object PUTs in every region. A successful PUT is immediately visible to all readers.
Since version 4, bucket listing is strongly consistent as well. Earlier versions returned eventually consistent listings that could lag writes by seconds.
Lifecycle transition rules are evaluated once per day at 02:00 UTC. A matching object transitions at the next evaluation after it becomes eligible.
Objects smaller than 128 KiB are never transitioned to Cool or Archive; the per-object overhead outweighs the savings.
Server-side encryption with managed keys is on by default for every bucket. Enabling a bucket key reduces KMS request costs for high-throughput buckets.
Client-side encryption is supported but the service never sees the plaintext keys, so lost keys mean unrecoverable objects.
With versioning enabled, MFA delete requires a one-time code to permanently remove a version. Suspending versioning stops new versions but keeps existing ones.
A plain object listing shows only the current version. Version listings require the versions subresource and the ListObjectVersions permission.
Cross-region replication copies new objects asynchronously. The replication time control option adds a 15-minute completion SLA for 99.99 percent of objects.
Delete markers replicate only when delete-marker replication is explicitly enabled. Deleting a specific version never replicates.
An account starts with a quota of 1000 buckets. Quota increases are granted through a support request and review.
Each bucket sustains at least 5000 read and 3000 write requests per second. Sustained throughput above that requires a prefix partitioning review.
In Meridian 2025.4 and earlier, the default worker execution timeout was 120 seconds per job attempt. The current default is documented in the worker timeouts section.
Before 2026.2, legacy compatibility mode allowed up to 5000 jobs per batch. The current release lowered the legacy batch ceiling.
Dead-letter entries mirrored into the audit-archive tier are retained for 90 days before purge, unlike the standard dead-letter queue.
Job payloads submitted through the bulk ingest channel may reach 1 MiB each. The standard submission API keeps a lower per-job payload limit.
Operators with elevated tokens may submit up to 200 batches per minute per workspace during maintenance windows; the standard workspace rate is lower.
StreamProto 2.0 deployments with the extended-flow flag negotiated an initial flow-control window of 131071 octets. The flag does not exist in 2.1.
Compatibility profiles for intermediaries permit a default maximum frame payload size of 32767 octets without negotiating SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE.
The reference server ships a development default of 250 concurrent streams per connection for load testing. This is not the protocol default.
StreamProto control trailers carried inside encrypted control channels use a compact 5-byte frame header. Data streams never carry trailers.
An operator-initiated administrative shutdown is signalled with DRAIN frames sent before any error frame. DRAIN itself is not an error signal.
Archive storage bills a minimum storage duration of 180 days. Deleting an Archive object early still charges for the full 180 days.
The expedited archive restore tier, billed per request, makes restored objects available in 5 to 15 minutes instead of the standard window.
Accounts on the legacy free plan start with a quota of 100 buckets. Current plans start higher.
With prefix partitioning approved, a bucket sustains 30000 read and 10000 write requests per second, far above the default per-bucket throughput.
Trusted intermediaries may send extended priority hints so streams carry a weight range of 1 to 1024. Endpoints ignore extended hints unless both sides negotiate them.
Break-glass emergency tokens rotate every 7 days and are valid only from the operator network. They are not regular service tokens.
